extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of formal logic, philosophers, and logicians
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and guidance for assessing the correctness, form, and philosophical status of syllogisms and related propositional forms, including handling of definitions, singular propositions, quantified predicates, and numerically definite premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish definitional from factual premises
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether a premise is a definition (part of the meaning of a term) or a statement of fact; a definitional premise does not serve as an empirical premise in proving a factual conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a premise is part of the definition (true by meaning), it cannot be the empirical premise that grounds a conclusion about reality. When premises include both a definition and a factual claim, the factual claim must be the one judged for truth; definitions merely fix meanings and should not be treated as empirical evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid attributing real properties to imaginary entities
rubrics_metrics.description: When reasoning about imaginary creatures or entities, predicates that would assert real properties must be qualified (e.g., 'imagined to breathe flame') to avoid illicitly implying the entity's reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reformulate predicates concerning imaginary things to indicate imagination rather than reality; failure to do so conflates make-believe with factual assertion and can render premises improperly factual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect equivocation and the need for knowledge of things
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether an argument 'turns wholly upon words' because key terms are used in different senses; this requires substantial knowledge of the subject-matter to judge whether apparent fallacies are genuine or only verbal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A critic should be cautious before declaring an argument merely verbal; many valid arguments rely on subtle 'unobvious links' between senses of terms that a less informed critic could mistake for equivocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Obversion and Equivalent Propositional Forms appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that certain changes of expression (e.g., affirming a proposition vs. denying its negative) preserve truth and can be used to test and transform propositions (Obversion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply rules of obversion and other equivalent propositional transformations (as discussed by Bain and others) to put propositions into equivalent forms that may make inference relations clearer or expose errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion rules (including Hamilton's form)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be able to convert propositions correctly (e.g., Sir W. Hamilton's suggested conversion: 'Some A is not B' → 'No B is some A').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the appropriate conversion for each categorical form to avoid mistaken reciprocal inferences; conversion is a basic corrective against inferring reciprocity when it doesn't hold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify oppositions among propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand relations among propositions — contraries, subtraries, contradictories, and subalternate — to evaluate consistency and entailment between statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these classical categories (examples given: All A is B vs No A is B, Some A is B vs Some A is not B, etc.) to check which propositions can co-exist and which are mutually exclusive or entail one another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat singular propositions cautiously in syllogisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether syllogisms involving singular propositions are genuine inferences or merely immediate/grammatical abbreviations of combined premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether singular-premise syllogisms add new information or simply reproduce parts of what is already asserted; do not automatically class singulars with universals for purposes of ratiocination without checking their logical role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for numerical/proportional quantification (De Morgan's numerically definite syllogism)
rubrics_metrics.description: When premises use terms like 'most' or give numerical proportions, use those proportions to compute definite minimal overlaps and thereby derive more precise conclusions (e.g., if 60% of B are C and 70% of B are A, at least 30% of B are both A and C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate 'most' and other proportionally definite premises into numerical relations where possible and apply combinatorial reasoning to obtain lower bounds on intersection sizes; recognize these inferences are legitimate but require numerical precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider quantification of the predicate (Hamilton's doctrine)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantifying the predicate (taking predicate quantity into account) creates additional valid propositional forms and can serve as a technical test of syllogistic correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use predicate quantification as a formal method to test ratiocination — it can produce more moods and allow conversion — but be aware of the critique that such forms may not reflect the actual mental content of ordinary propositions; treat them as a formal tool rather than a psychological description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose axioms appropriate to the logic's purpose (dictum de omni vs 'nota notae' axiom)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select the foundational axiom suitable for the intended logic: the dictum de omni is apt for formal logic of consistency, whereas an axiom like 'Nota notae est nota rei ipsius' (the mark of a mark is the mark of the thing) is argued to be more appropriate for deductive logic aiming at discovery of truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retain the dictum de omni as the basis for formal/logical consistency work, but adopt the 'nota notae' style axiom when analyzing deduction as a route to truth; recognize both have value in their respective domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make limitations explicit when transferring attributes via middle terms
rubrics_metrics.description: When transferring a property from A to C through middle term B, explicitly account for the fact that A and C may each share B with other things; failure to limit transfer can falsely imply co-extensionality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the mistake of inferring reciprocity or co-extensiveness; ensure the syllogistic transfer includes proper limiting clauses or conversion steps to represent partial coincidences among classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match syllogistic figure to argumentative purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Different figures of syllogism are suited to different tasks: first figure for discovering/proving properties, second for distinguishing things, third for instances/exceptions, fourth for excluding species of a genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing or evaluating an argument, choose the figure that aligns with the aim (property discovery, distinction, instance identification, exclusion) and check that the figure's axioms and canons are properly applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use majors and minors as interpretive safeguards, not necessities
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat the syllogistic major and minor as conventions that interpret general principles and identify the requisite kind of likeness; they are precautions against error rather than strictly necessary components of reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the minor specifies the precise kind of likeness required to apply the major; recognize that informal reasoning may omit explicit major/minor formulations, but doing so increases the risk of mistaken induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express general propositions to reflect inductive function ('Any man is mortal')
rubrics_metrics.description: Formulate general propositions in a way that makes clear their role as warrants for inferring from particulars to particulars (e.g., preferring 'Any man is mortal' to 'All men are mortal').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrase generalizations to exhibit that they vouch for particular-to-particular inferences; this clarifies the inductive character of many general statements and avoids the appearance that a general assertion is itself the empirical proof of individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid petitio principii (circular proof by a general that presupposes the conclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not treat a general proposition as the proof of a particular when the general itself presupposes that particular; ensure that the evidence supporting a generalization is independent of the specific cases it is used to prove.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check the grounds of the general assertion; if the general was formed from the same cases it is then used to prove, recognize and avoid circularity. Require external or prior justification for general premises when they are used to prove particulars.
